text_narrative: The steward's clerk has the roll open on the trestle and cannot make the entries balance. Fourteen tenants presented, thirteen fines entered, and the margin of the membrane carries a fifteenth name in a different ink. Outside, the tenants stand in the yard with their strips of parchment. He turns the membrane over, finds the missing fine written on the back in the same different ink, and sets down a cross beside it.
text_nonnarrative: A defective roll was distinguished by where the entry stood, not by whose hand set it there. An entry in the margin of a membrane counted as good where the same ink ran through the body; a fine written on the back of a membrane was of a second class, admitted only on the clerk's oath. The count of tenants presented bore on the remedy and never on the class. Parchment quality bore on neither.

text_narrative: They talk in the vestry still about the year the overseers questioned a woman named Alys Prendle for three sittings and could not settle where she belonged. She had been hired at one place by the year, married in a second, and had rented at eight pounds in a third. Every answer she gave was true and every answer moved her parish. In the end the clerk wrote down all three and left it.
text_nonnarrative: Settlement is determined by the last head that applies and not by the number of heads a person can show. Being hired for a year in one parish, being married in a second and having rented above ten pounds in a third are independent grounds, of which the latest governs. Answers given at three sittings weigh no more than answers given at one. The entry of the overseers bears on proof, never on the ground.

text_narrative: There was a harbour clerk who would sign no bill of health he had not read aloud, and a ship came in one autumn with a clean bill in a language nobody at the office knew. The clerk read it aloud all the same, syllable by syllable, and the words made a shape in the room that the lamps went round. He signed it, and the ship lay in the roads forty days anyway.
text_nonnarrative: A bill of health is graded clean, touched or foul, and the grade attaches to the harbour of issue rather than to the ship. An untranslated bill is not foul; it falls outside the grades and is held unclassed for want of an office copy in a known language. The clerk's signature bears on admissibility and not on the grade. Forty days in the roads follow from the grade alone, whatever the cargo.

text_narrative: In the second year after the incumbent's death, a schedule of dilapidations was drawn on the parsonage house and its outbuildings. Twenty-two items were listed, of which nine touched the barn roof alone. The valuers put the whole at eleven pounds four shillings and set the figure against the estate. The successor refused the barn items on the ground that the roof had been thatched with reed against a covenant naming straw.
text_nonnarrative: Dilapidation is classed by whether an item restores or improves, and not by the sum a valuer sets against it. Want of repair to a parsonage roof is one class; departure from a covenant, as thatch of reed where straw is named, is a second, independent of the first. Outbuildings fall under the same classes as the house. The total in pounds and shillings bears on the charge to an estate, never on the class.

text_narrative: The stamp in the inspector's box is not the stamp that left the county office, and Ferrers knows it without knowing how. Same crown, same letter, same worn place at the rim. But the impression it leaves on lead comes up shallow on one side, the way the old inspector's always did, and the old inspector has been three years in the ground. She stamps a second weight and looks at that too.
text_nonnarrative: Verification depended on the impression and not on the instrument that made it. A shallow impression in the lead of a weight was one class of defect, curable by restamping; a crown or county letter differing from the pattern held at the office was a second, and no impression of that kind counted at all. Wear at the rim of a stamp bore on the cause. The inspector's own book bore on neither class.

text_narrative: A registry of the county surveyor's office was rebuilt during the spring recess and the pigeonholes recut to a smaller size. Eleven thousand bundles were moved in nine days by four clerks working from a written plan. Two hundred and six bundles were afterwards found in holes not answering to their marks, all of them in the range nearest the door, and the plan for that range was never produced.
text_nonnarrative: A pigeonhole registry is carried on two independent orders. Bundles sit in holes by a running number, and the subject index is a separate sequence of slips referring to that number. Retrieval time is a function of the index alone and of the depth of a hole, not of the size of the collection. Without the slips the holes are unsearchable, and without the holes the slips point nowhere.

text_narrative: When the first archive was raised, the keepers were given no names for its rooms and no numbers for its shelves, and everything in it was found by memory alone. The last keeper wrote a mark on one bundle before she went, three letters and a figure, and the mark held. After her the rooms took letters and the shelves took figures, and nothing in the archive was ever again found by remembering.
text_nonnarrative: A shelf mark is a composite of three fields: room, press and position, each independent of the others in what it can be changed to. Its stability rests on the building and not on the contents, so a bundle keeps its mark while it keeps its place. Reshelving breaks the third field only. Any mark whose room letter is absent stands in no fixed relation to the rest of the sequence.

text_narrative: Three market days in a row the tallyman's counterfoils come back short. On the first day the book is one leaf light and the stub for it is missing too, which is possible. On the second the stub is there and the leaf gone, which is not. On the third he sits with both halves of the book open on his knees at the gate and lets the queue wait behind him.
text_nonnarrative: A counterfoil book is two records on one sheet of paper, divided by a perforation and numbered alike on both sides of it. The strength of the arrangement lies in that shared number, which is printed before issue and cannot be altered on one half alone. A missing leaf is detectable from its stub; a missing stub is detectable from nothing inside the book. Loose leaves are outside the system altogether.

text_narrative: The rod passed from the widow's hand to the steward's and then to her son's, and the whole business took less time than the walk from the church. Nobody in the hall said the word sale. The steward entered a surrender and an admittance on two lines of the roll, took the fine in coin from a purse the son had ready, and gave the rod back to the bailiff to keep.
text_nonnarrative: Three tenures are distinguished here, and the middle one is neither of the others. Freehold is held of nobody and passes by deed. Copyhold is held of a manor and passes by surrender and admittance entered on a roll, the rod and the fine belonging to the form and not to the substance. Leasehold is a term of years, distinguished from both by having an end fixed at its beginning.

text_narrative: Everybody in the hundred knows the jury list for the upper division is wrong, and nobody will say which way. Forty-one names where there were fifty-three the year before. The high constable's returns are all in the same hand, including the two parishes that sent nothing that year. A clerk who asks about it at the sessions house is told the books for that division are out for binding.
text_nonnarrative: Two lists were kept and only one of them was public. The general list held every man qualified by property in a division, and was open at the parish chest. The panel was drawn from it for a given sitting and was not open at all, being distinguished from the general list by having a date. A third paper, the constable's return, was the material of the first and belonged to neither.

text_narrative: There was a chancellor's daughter who was given the counterseal to keep and told never to press it alone. For a year she carried it on a cord and pressed nothing. In the second year she pressed it into cold wax, and the wax took the small device on the back and none of the great one on the front, and the sheet was worth a manor to whoever held it.
text_nonnarrative: A counterseal is not a lesser seal but a second impression on the reverse of the same wax, and the pair is one authentication in two parts. The great seal stands alone on writs of the highest kind, where no counterseal is used. A signet is a third thing, distinguished from both by being personal to a holder and by leaving no impression on the reverse at all.

text_narrative: In the fifth year of the Commutation, the surveyors of the western division finished a map of nine hundred and four numbered parcels and lodged three copies, one of them in a chest that would not lock. The apportionment was read in the church over two days. Four occupiers found their names against parcels on the wrong side of the brook, and the brook itself was drawn a chain out of place.
text_nonnarrative: The parish lies in two unequal parts on either side of a brook, and the larger part is the wetter. Numbered parcels run from the church outward, so that the low ground carries the lowest numbers. Three lanes cross the brook, of which the middle one is metalled. The glebe is a single block on the eastern rise, and the common is above it, unnumbered and undivided on the map.

text_narrative: The bounds had been walked every seventh year since anyone could remember, and Ottilie had walked six of them. This one went wrong at the third mark. Not moved. The stone was where it had always been, and the ash beside it was where it had always been, but the two of them had changed places about the path, and nobody else in the line of forty seemed to notice.
text_nonnarrative: Eleven marks stand on the boundary, and no two of them are of one kind. Four are stones, three are trees, two are the corners of walls, and the remaining pair are holes in the ground. The line between the fifth and sixth marks is under water at every season. On the northern side the boundary is also the road; elsewhere it is a hedge with the ditch on the outer face.

text_narrative: The land office at Vesk Terrace issues a renumbering of the second district and eleven hundred holdings change their designations in one afternoon. Two adjoining plots receive the same number, 2-441, one on the register and one on the map. The holder of the lower plot lodges a query the same day. The office replies that the map governs, and the map is the copy that has not yet been corrected.
text_nonnarrative: The district lay in four quarters about a central square, and the numbering had its origin at the north-west corner of each. Odd numbers ran along the inner faces of the blocks, even numbers along the outer. Holdings on the square itself bore no quarter prefix and were the only ones so distinguished. The two streets running out to the west were numbered from the far end inward, against the rule everywhere else.

text_narrative: In the age when houses were counted by their fires, the counters went out with tallies of hazel and were told to write down smoke. A house with two fires was written twice and a house with none was not written at all. So the poor went out of the record like breath off a window, and the counters came back with a country smaller than the one they had walked.
text_nonnarrative: Hearth numbers vary more between neighbouring parishes than between one region and another. Half the houses in the returns are entered with a single hearth, and the exempt are a fifth of the whole in some places and none at all in others. Two-thirds of the spread is accounted for by how the exempt are treated rather than by any difference in building. Enumerators disagree most about outbuildings with a chimney.

text_narrative: Three times in five years the assessor came to the same house on the hill road and three times the number of windows was different. On the first visit he counted nineteen. On the second, fourteen, seven of them newly bricked and the mortar still pale. On the third he counted fourteen again and then walked round to the yard side, where a scullery had grown a window since the spring.
text_nonnarrative: Window counts differ more between two assessments of one house than between houses of a like size. A third of the dwellings in the schedules stand at the threshold figure exactly, which is more than chance would put there. Bricked openings account for most of the movement downward; additions at the rear, for nearly all of the movement up. Assessors in the same district return figures a fifth apart on average.

text_narrative: Candle end, and the rate book is still open at the letter M. The assistant overseer works down the column with a wet thumb, entering the sums the vestry set in April, and the column will not come to the total at the foot. Eleven shillings out. He goes back to the top, finds a house entered twice under two spellings of one name, and rules one of them through.
text_nonnarrative: Rateable values within one parish are spread more widely than the rents they stand on. The median assessment in the books is a fifth of a rack rent, and the highest tenth of properties carries above half the sum levied. Duplicate entries under variant spellings are commoner in the earlier books than in the later, and account for a small part of the difference between a book's total and its column sums.

text_narrative: In the old parish they will tell of the banns that were called three times to an empty church, because the couple named in them had never asked. The clerk swore he had the entry in his own hand and could not say who set it there. Both persons named came from villages a day apart and had never met. They met at the third calling and the thing went forward.
text_nonnarrative: Banns are a public notice of an intended marriage, characterised by publication three times over, on separate weeks, in the parishes of both parties. Their effect is negative: they create no obligation and only remove one impediment, that of secrecy. Publication in the wrong parish is of no effect, and the period of validity is short and fixed, running three months from the last calling. A licence is the alternative instrument.

text_narrative: There was a heron who kept a notary's office at the ford and would protest anything brought to him, for a fish. A vole brought a bill that nobody had refused, and the heron protested it all the same, and drew the instrument up with his own long hand. The vole's bill was afterwards worth less than the fish. The heron said the paper was correct, and it was.
text_nonnarrative: A protest is an instrument recording that a bill has been presented and not honoured, characterised by being made by a public officer rather than by a party. Its force is evidential, and depends on the presentment it records; a protest of a bill never refused proves nothing but its regularity. The form is narrow and fixed by the office, and the wording of the noting is not at the drawer's choice.

text_narrative: In the ninth year of the transit office, endorsements were required on every leaf of a passage book rather than on the last, and the books grew to forty leaves. A traveller of the outer stations arrived with thirty-one endorsements and one leaf missing at the fold. The clerk of the day entered a note of the gap, stamped the following leaf twice, and let the passage stand on the strength of the note.
text_nonnarrative: An endorsement is a mark added to a document complete in itself, characterised by standing outside the text it qualifies. Its authority is derivative: it can restrict a passage or extend it in time, and can do nothing where the underlying instrument is void. Continuity of leaves is therefore essential to the whole, since an endorsement proves only what it touches. A note of a missing leaf is itself an endorsement of the lowest order.

text_narrative: The rough minutes are in pencil on both sides of a folded sheet and the fair copy is due at noon. Twelve resolutions, and the eleventh has a word crossed through that might be adjourned and might be adopted. Halbin has been clerk for nine years and has never asked the chairman anything. He writes adjourned, in a round hand, and leaves the rough sheet in the book where anyone can find it.
text_nonnarrative: Minutes were to be engrossed in a bound book with ruled margins, in one hand throughout a meeting, and were not to be written on both sides of a loose sheet for the fair copy. Erasure was forbidden; a word struck through was required to remain legible, with the substitution above it. Rough notes were permitted to be destroyed only where the engrossment was signed. No resolution was to stand unnumbered.

text_narrative: A stock of unstamped paper was found in the flooded offices of the old revenue house and carried to the market at Ilder Cross. Nine reams were legible and dry. The market keeper ruled that any sheet bearing the old impression counted as stamped in the market's own registers, and that plain sheets did not. Two traders produced sheets with the impression drawn on in ink, and both sheets were refused.
text_nonnarrative: Instruments are to be written on sheets bearing an impressed stamp of the value fixed for the class, and the impression is required to be struck in advance of any writing on the sheet. A drawn or printed imitation is permitted for no purpose. Where a sheet is damaged, an office copy on a fresh stamp is to be substituted. Nothing written across an impression is to be read as part of the instrument.

text_narrative: When the first poll was taken in the valley towns, the names were written down in the order the voices came, and the book was left open on a table in the square for as long as the season lasted. Whoever read it aloud found the order changed. Not the names, but the order. The clerks held that a book read too often begins to arrange itself, and stopped leaving it open.
text_nonnarrative: Poll books are read as records of opinion, and they are better read as records of order. What they fix is the sequence in which men came forward, which is a fact about a town's arrangement of itself, not about anyone's mind. It is fair to object that the votes are also there on the page. So they are, and they are the part a later reader can least often use.

text_narrative: Four times this year the district clerk has renamed the same lane. In March it is Back Row, because that is what the rate book has. In June it is Chapel Walk, because the chapel trustees ask. In August it is Back Row again, on a petition of nine householders. In November he leaves the plate off the wall altogether and writes both names in the register, one above the other.
text_nonnarrative: Street names are worth less as description than as a record of who was asking. A name that describes, like the back of something, dates from a time when a district had one centre; a name that commemorates dates from a time when it had a committee. It is said that either kind will serve for finding a house. Either will, which is why the choice between them is never about finding.

text_narrative: The register had been rebound and the gutter took the last letter of every line on the left-hand page. Verrin held it under the lamp at an angle and read what he could. Four entries in a hand that leaned backward, all in one week of one year, and none of them in the index at the front. The rest of the volume leaned the other way and was indexed to the leaf.
text_nonnarrative: Secretary hand: the ordinary book hand of the older registers, upright and heavily abbreviated. Current hand: the later cursive, distinguished by the joining of every letter in a word. Gutter loss: text that was carried into the fold of a rebound volume and was thereafter illegible. Interleaf: a sheet that was added at binding and bore no original entry. Reversed leaning: any hand sloping backward, a mark of one writer.

text_narrative: Anyone in the office will tell a new clerk about the deed with the third interlineation, and they tell it the same way every time. Two words above the line in the habendum, initialled twice in the margin by the same two hands. The engrossing clerk who wrote them has been dead a long while and the family still holds the land. Nobody has ever needed to argue about the words themselves.
text_nonnarrative: Engrossment: the fair copy of an instrument, written for execution and not for revision. Interlineation: any words inserted above a line of an engrossment, which were required to be initialled in the margin. Rasure: a place where the surface of the parchment had been scraped, distinguished from an ordinary blot by its thinness. Habendum: the clause that limited the estate granted. Vacat: a marginal note that a passage was void.

text_narrative: There was a clerk of the rolls who could not write his own name and had held the office nine years by memory alone. Every man who subscribed the roll before him did so twice, once on the parchment and once aloud, and the clerk kept the second copy in his head. When the roll was lost in a wet spring he recited four hundred names in order to a boy with a pen.
text_nonnarrative: Subscription meant, in that part, the writing of a name on the roll itself and not on any schedule annexed to it. Where a subscriber was unable to write, a mark made in the presence of the officer was of the same effect. A roll wanting the officer's own subscription at the foot was of no effect, whatever it otherwise contained. No provision of that part touched oaths taken outside a roll.

text_narrative: In the seventh year of the register, memorials of eleven thousand deeds were enrolled in the county office and the index to them was left a year behind. A purchaser of land in the northern division found two memorials of the same deed, entered on different days by different hands, with the parcels described differently in each. The registrar enrolled a third memorial reciting both, and the matter rested there.
text_nonnarrative: A memorial was, under that head, a summary of a deed subscribed by a party and enrolled, and was not the deed. Where two memorials of one deed stood on the register, neither displaced the other and both were notice. A memorial was required to name the parcels; one that did not was notice of nothing. Enrolment gave priority by date of entry and by no other measure.

text_narrative: Forty-one beasts on the moor and the stint is thirty-eight, and Maren cannot make the three extra belong to anybody. She counts them again from the gate. The same forty-one, and the three at the back are the ones whose colour will not hold in the mind afterwards. Somebody's, then. She writes thirty-eight in the herd book, as every reeve before her has done, and closes it. The moor keeps its own count.
text_nonnarrative: A beast is lawfully on the common only where its owner holds a stint and the stint is not full. Two commoners may not make up one stint between them; a half stint is a holding and not a share. Beasts of a kind not named in the stint are outside it, whatever their number, and no count of them is a count of the stint. Levancy and couchancy bind independently of number.

text_narrative: A carrier of the eastern district applies for a licence in two names, his own and that of a partnership dissolved in the spring, and the clerk of licences declines both applications on one sheet. The carrier's waggon and horses are the same in each. A second application in the partnership name alone is entered on the following day and stands, on the ground that the partnership's registration has not been struck out.
text_nonnarrative: An application was in order only where one person or one firm was named in it, and a licence held in one name did not cover a vehicle worked in another. Two applications on one sheet were a single application and were refused together. A firm whose registration stood undeleted was a person for this purpose, whatever its condition otherwise. Refusal was not a decision on the vehicle and did not touch it.

text_narrative: In the first years of the wardships, the makers of the law required that everything belonging to a child be written down while the child was small, so that nothing could be added or taken. One inventory came back with a line for a thing the clerks could not name, between the beds and the linen, and it was left on the roll unpriced for the whole of that minority.
text_nonnarrative: A ward's inventory ran to five heads, of which the household stuff was always the longest. Beds and their furniture stood at the top, priced by the tester; linen came under the second head, by the pair; brass and pewter under the third, by weight; the stock on the ground under the fourth, valued by the head. Debts owing were listed at the foot and never valued.

text_narrative: Twice the incumbent tried to make the terrier agree with the ground, and twice he gave it up. In the first summer he walked the four closes with the old paper and found a fifth close in it that nobody could point to. In the second he found the fifth close, under furze, and no mention in the paper of the pond that was plainly there. He wrote both facts at the foot.
text_nonnarrative: A terrier held four kinds of thing and no more. The glebe land itself stood first, close by close, with the acreage of each and the names of the abutters. The house and its outbuildings were described by bay and by the material of the walls. The moveable goods of the church were counted by number. Rights in kind, such as timber or turf, were named without measure, and rents were not entered.

text_narrative: The appraisers have finished the upstairs rooms and are sitting on the stairs with the list between them. Forty-two items, and the sum at the foot is under twenty pounds. Everything in the house is old and nothing in it is worth anything, which is the third house of this kind on the street this year. The younger appraiser turns back to the first page and looks at the entry for the writing desk.
text_nonnarrative: Probate valuations were the least useful of the household records, and their defenders never met the reason. What passed for a price in them was a figure at which nobody had offered anything; the appraisers had no buyer and no instruction but to be low. Comparison between two such lists was therefore comparison of two habits. The best of them were the ones that described an object well and priced it badly.

text_narrative: Everyone in the village had a version of what the commissioners did with the north field in the second year of the war, and none of the versions agreed with the award. The award said forty acres to the depot and an exchange of twenty-two elsewhere. The old men said sixty and nothing back. A woman who had kept the tally of the hay crop said the award was right and nobody believed her.
text_nonnarrative: Awards were read for their maps and dismissed for their prose, which was the wrong way round. The schedules of exchange were the substance: a plain table of who lost what and took what instead, in a form that admitted no rhetoric. Critics held that such tables told nothing of how the thing was felt. They told nothing of it, and were the only part that could be checked against a field.

text_narrative: There was a master who bound an apprentice for a term of seven years and would not say when the term had begun. The indenture was in two parts, and the boy's half gave no date where the master's half had one. Every quarter day the boy asked, and every quarter day the master counted on his fingers and said not yet. The boy grew old in the shop, waiting to be free.
text_nonnarrative: The puzzle whether an indenture was one instrument or two was not idle. Both parts were engrossed together and severed, so that each was the whole in form and the half in fact; if the parts disagreed, there was no third document to appeal to. Treating the pair as one thing left the disagreement unexplained. Treating them as two left the term of an apprenticeship a matter of which half a reader held.

text_narrative: In the twelfth year of the Assembly's charter, admissions to the freedom of the city were made by three roads at once, and the register kept them in one column. Forty-one came by service, twenty by patrimony, and nine by redemption at a fee set that year. One man came by two roads on the same day, service and patrimony both, and was entered twice with a line drawn between the entries.
text_nonnarrative: Freedom of a city was either a status or a bundle of permissions, and the two accounts pulled apart at the double entry. If it was a status, a man could not hold it twice and one of the two entries was surplus. If it was a bundle, he could, and the register was right to record both roads by which the bundle was got. Neither account made the fee intelligible.

text_narrative: The tallies had come in short again and Wenceslas had counted them three times before the light went. Ninety-one sticks for a hundred and four holdings. Somebody was paying in coin and taking no stick, which was allowed, or somebody was taking two sticks for one payment, which was not, and there was no way to tell the two apart from a heap of hazel on a table by lamplight.
text_nonnarrative: The count of tallies stood in no fixed proportion to the sum received, since a payment in coin left no stick and a stick could be split. Error in the total varied as the square root of the number of holdings where the notches were cut by one hand, and faster than that where they were cut by several. Beyond about two hundred holdings the tally ceased to be a measure of anything.

text_narrative: A manifest lodged at the outport of Grennick lists ninety casks inward and the tide surveyor finds ninety-one in the shed. The extra cask carries the same mark as the fortieth and the same weight to the ounce. Both are opened in the presence of two officers and both hold the same quantity of the same oil. The surveyor enters ninety-one in the book and rules the total twice.
text_nonnarrative: Discrepancy between a manifest and a landing was proportional to the number of packages and not to their value, the constant being a property of the marking practice at the port of lading. Duty, being reckoned on weight, moved with the gross and not with the count, so that the two errors were of different orders. Beyond a certain size of cargo the relation broke down and the count governed nothing.

text_narrative: When the first charters were granted, each was made of four parts that had to travel together: the words, the seal, the cord that joined them, and a bag of the town's own earth sewn to the foot. A town that lost the bag kept its market and lost its name for it. The words alone were held to be worth nothing at all, and were copied freely by anyone who could write.
text_nonnarrative: A charter of market had three parts standing in a fixed relation. The text was a single membrane, written on one side, with a turn-up at the foot. The seal hung from a cord or a tag passed through that turn-up and was no part of the text. Warranty clauses stood at the end of the text and were absent in the shorter forms, where the witness list took their place.

text_narrative: Three times in one voyage the mate has to go up to the bond office with the same bundle of papers. The first time the warrant is right and the landing account is not. The second time both are right and the officer's counterpart is out of the book. The third time he takes all three halves at once, and the clerk keeps the middle one and gives back two.
text_nonnarrative: A bonded entry was a set of three documents of unequal size. The entry proper was a folio sheet, ruled in six columns, of which the last was left blank at lodging. The warrant was a quarter of that size and bore the marks and numbers only. The officer's counterpart was bound into a book and could not be separated from it. A fourth paper, the delivery order, was absent in warehousing entries.
